newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: Ten-year-bond futures and three-month PIBOR settled higher on Monday, supported by an accord by EU leaders in Amsterdam allowing approval of a fiscal disciplinary pact seen as vital to the launch of the euro.
A strong tone to U.S. Treasuries also helped underpin the market, analysts said.
With the EU stability pact approved, analysts said the key focus was Tuesday's heavy calendar of U.S. economic data on data that includes consumer prices and industrial production.
"We think the data will be fairly positive for the market," said bond analyst Nathalie Fillet of Banque Paribas.
The stability pact was approved along with a French-backed resolution aimed at boosting employment and growth which at the same time committing the EU to aim for balanced or surplus budgets.
The deal put the EU's drive for a single currency by 1999 back on track after a week of uncertainty.

"I cannot see how anyone can lose face with a resolution saying more jobs and growth," said one analyst. "It's non-controversial. What would have been controversial was a commitment to infrastructure projects costing billions of euros which would have been a bad idea given the budgetary restraints.
The market was supported on Monday by continued positive reaction to Friday's better than expected producer price index.

The September 10-year bond future contract climbed sharply in morning trade on a wave of short-covering to hit 129.52 but then retraced to settle at 129.20, up 28 basis points. September PIBOR finished three basis points higher at 96.59.

Analysts said market-friendly U.S. data on Tuesday was expected to push the market higher but gains would be capped by uncertainty over an inaugural policy speech to be made by new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin to the National Assembly on Thursday.
"If the figures match expectations or are better, the notionnel should climb with the T-bond but should not go higher than today's best level of 129.52," said one trader.
Analysts said they did not expect any major announcements by Jospin as the new government would not have completed its audit of French finances.
"There's a risk he will just announce minor things and all the major decisions will be left over for the autumn," one said.
At the same time, economists said they did not expect Jospin to be inclined to boost the 1997 French deficit.

"Allowing for slower growth in first quarter, we are maintaining our forecast that the new government will have an inherited a 3.2 percent deficit (to GDP)," said Marie Owens-Thomsen of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
She said she expected that "all new measures announced will be fully financed either through spending cuts or a higher CSG," which is a tax on most income.
She said that she believed Jospin would announce a number of measures on Thursday that would have a media impact but that "would be short on budgetary impact".

She expected the bottom value added tax rate, which applies to such basic goods as food, to be cut to five percent from five and half percent, at least a four percent rise in the minimum wage. She said that public services wages could rise by two percent.
"This would go a long way to satisfying voter demands and would not cost that much," she said.
Owens-Thomsen said she expected Jospin to say the Socialists' campaign commitment to create 700,000 new youth jobs would be implemented gradually over the five-year life of the parliament.
She also expected him to say that his pledge to cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 hours would be done in negotiation with individual businesses.
